item.title: Grand Theft Porter: Thieves Steal 800 Barrels of Guinness in Britain
item.description:
The police in the county of Cheshire in northwestern England are investigating the theft of two trailers of Guinness beer from an industrial park.

Two trucks entered the depot on Monday and hauled away trailers containing 800 barrels of the creamy dark stout, the authorities said.

“It is famously said that ‘Guinness is good for you,’ but that is only the case when it has been bought and paid for,” Detective Sgt. Gary McClatchey of the Cheshire Constabulary said in a statement on Thursday.

The police will settle for “nothing less than the full recovery of all the items stolen,” he added.

Diageo, the British beverage company that owns Guinness, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A spokesman for the Cheshire police said on Friday that there were no updates in the investigation.

Precisely what the thieves planned to do with their large stash of stout was unclear. The police said the value of the stolen beer was 115,000 pounds, or about $155,000.

The truck drivers were believed to men, the police said. They appealed for any witnesses to come forward and for motorists to review dashboard camera footage in hopes of catching the brew burglars.

The theft came on the heels of another high-profile beer heist in the United States. Last month, Pabst Blue Ribbon said that 40,000 pounds of its beer had been stolen from a distribution center in Montclair, Calif., a haul that the local police said was worth $25,000.

Pabst offered a reward on social media to anyone who helped them recover the lost beer.

item.title: Timothy Carney, Diplomat Who Went Places Others Avoided, Dies at 82
item.description:
Timothy Carney, a diplomat who relished difficult assignments in war-torn countries and pushed against bureaucratic restrictions, died on Aug. 10 at his home in Cambridge, Mass. He was 82.

His death, from cancer, was confirmed by his wife, Victoria Butler.

In a State Department career that took him from Saigon and Phnom Penh during the Vietnam War, to South Africa during the final years of apartheid, to ambassadorships in Sudan and Haiti as those countries disintegrated, to Iraq after the U.S. invasion, Mr. Carney proved willing to challenge conventional thinking and to go places other diplomats avoided.

He foresaw the looming menace of the Khmer Rouge dictatorship in Cambodia in the mid-1970s, and engaged with Afrikaners in the mid-1980s, convinced they were opening up to the idea of majority rule in South Africa. He opposed closing the U.S. embassy in Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, in 1996 while Osama Bin Laden established himself there — the closure deprived America of a valuable listening post. He was skeptical of the former Haiti president Jean-Bertrand Aristide, seen by many in Washington as a valuable ally, as Mr. Aristide prepared to retake power. In Iraq, Mr. Carney was publicly disgusted with the absence of American planning.

Colleagues said he didn’t hesitate to engage with U.S. foes, believing that to be the diplomats’ best role. “He wasn’t afraid of anybody,” the former U.S. ambassador Robin Raphel, who knew Mr. Carney for decades, said in an interview.

“You don’t make deals with your friends, you make deals with your enemies,” Ms. Raphel said, describing Mr. Carney as “pro-engagement in a way that makes perfect sense.” She added: “Serious people paid attention to him.”

Unusually for a diplomat, Mr. Carney insisted on seeing things for himself, even at the cost of incurring the wrath of his superiors.

As Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, was being rocketed by rebels in 1972, Mr. Carney — then a junior official in the U.S. embassy — jumped into a car with a Cambodian journalist and soon found “a little kid” who “had been chopped up by a chunk of casing from this 122 mm rocket, and was dead,” Mr. Carney told an interviewer in 2002 for a State Department oral history project.

Undeterred, “we heard a lot of automatic weapons fire from further south,” he said, “and we drove down there to see what was going on.”

The next day, he reported all of it to his bosses at the embassy. They were horrified.

“One didn’t do that,” Mr. Carney told the interviewer in 2002. “You weren’t supposed to put yourself at risk, which struck me as a very bizarre way to do foreign affairs reporting in a war. You have to get out, meet people, and be out of the embassy as much as you possibly could.”

That approach — leaving the embassy — was, and remains, untypical for State Department officials. In an era of heightened security concerns, American diplomats typically stay behind the embassy’s Marine-guarded walls, venturing out only for official events

“He was where no other foreign service officer would be,” Elizabeth Becker, a journalist with extensive reporting experience in Cambodia, said in an interview. “He treated Cambodians with a kind of dignity I did not see from others.”

In April 1975, with the murderous Khmer Rouge closing in, he drove to the prime minister’s house to urge government ministers to evacuate via helicopter. “Nope,” he recalled. “Only one went with us.”

He followed the same path 10 years later in South Africa, where as a political counselor at the U.S. embassy in Pretoria, he went to parties with Afrikaners, some of whom defended apartheid, while meeting others who were “serious, engaging, ruthless, but they had the real interest” in ending it, unlike more outwardly liberal South Africans who he believed paid lip service to change.

“No matter how unstable the political environment and how tense relations could be, Tim always maintained the highest level of professionalism and tenacity,” former President Bill Clinton, who appointed Mr. Carney as ambassador in Sudan and Haiti, wrote on Facebook after his death. Mr. Clinton added that Mr. Carney “always believed that diplomacy was the essential key to reducing instability and promoting peace and prosperity.”

When Mr. Clinton sent Mr. Carney to Sudan in 1995, the country was a safe harbor for Islamist terrorists, and boiling with insurgency. Bin Laden had found refuge there after leaving Saudi Arabia in 1991. For Mr. Carney it was an ideal spot from which to gauge the terrorist threat ahead.

But officials in Washington, led by Susan Rice, the National Security Council senior director for African Affairs at the time, were nervous about threats to the diplomats in Khartoum, and moved them to Nairobi early in 1996.

For Mr. Carney, it was a big mistake. He had been keeping an eye on Mr. Bin Laden but could no longer do so. “We took our eye off the ball,” he later told Roger Cohen of The New York Times. “We did not know what was happening in Khartoum, a center of extremist Islam.”

The same bluntness characterized his response to the chaos of Haiti, where he arrived as ambassador in January 1998 — “no trees except at the embassy residence” he said in the State Department oral history interview — and quickly took the measure of Mr. Aristide, who was regarded with indulgence on Capitol Hill.

“He was more of the same,” Mr. Carney told the state department interviewer. “He himself certainly tolerates corruption as a way of manipulating people. Interesting.”

Timothy Michael Carney was born on July 12, 1944, in St. Joseph, Mo., one of three children of Col. Clement Carney, a career army officer who was a judge in the Judge Advocate General Corps, and Jane (Byrne) Carney, an English teacher. The family moved often when Mr. Carney was growing up, and two of those years were spent in Taipei.

He graduated from Christian Brothers High School in St. Joseph in 1962, and from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology with a Bachelor of Science in 1966.

His first foreign service job came the following year with a junior posting at the embassy in Vietnam, and from 1969 to 1971 he was posted to the embassy in Lesotho.

After his tour in Cambodia ended in 1975, Mr. Carney studied at Cornell University, served in Washington on the State Department’s Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia desk, and was appointed to the U.S. mission in Thailand from 1979 to 1983.

During the 1990s, Mr. Carney undertook several missions for the United Nations, including as adviser to the U.N. representative in Somalia in 1993.

Mr. Carney retired from the State Department in December 1999. He returned to government service for several months in 2003 as a member of the Office of Reconstruction and Humanitarian Assistance, the agency established under the Department of Defense to help reconstruct Iraq.

He left Baghdad after two months, frustrated by what the writer David Rieff called a “dialogue of the deaf between ORHA officials and the U.S. military on the ground in Iraq.” He returned to Iraq for several months in 2007, and assisted the State Department in Kabul in 2009.

In addition to his wife, a journalist and writer, whom he married in 1983, Mr. Carney is survived by his sister, Sheri Carney; his daughter, Anne Carney, from his previous marriage with Demaz Tep Baker; and two grandchildren.

“Tim was very deeply committed everywhere he served,” Ms. Butler said in an interview. “Everywhere we went he got to know the people where we lived. He believed very strongly in soft power versus hard power. He was an old school kind of diplomat.”

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: German Far-Right Surges, in Threat to Postwar Taboo on Extremists in Power
item.description:
In 77 years of postwar German democracy, no far-right political party has ever won a state election. That streak could end on Sunday in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the Alternative for Germany party is riding a wave of voter anger at immigration, economic stagnation and the centrist parties that have long governed the nation.

The party, known as the AfD, has been designated a “suspected” extremist group by German intelligence agencies. But it has surged in recent years and now leads national polls.

Saxony-Anhalt is the party’s stronghold: Surveys suggest it could win enough votes on Sunday to claim a majority of seats in the state Parliament, allowing it to form a government there without the support of centrist and leftist parties that refuse to work with it. Whether that happens depends on a combination of variables, which makes it difficult to say whether the party will prevail or fall just short.

If the AfD does take power, it would jolt Germany’s democracy, which was built after World War II from the rubble of Nazism with safeguards meant to block any party deemed extreme from ever running a state or national government.

“If a radical right-wing party came into a government in Germany, it would have a completely different meaning than if it happened in another country in the European Union,” Friedrich Merz, the chancellor, said in July.

These concerns are partly rooted in the dog-whistle comments about Nazism from some party leaders, some of whom have belittled the Holocaust and used Nazi slogans. Some are close to Russia, prompting concerns that they might pass national secrets to Moscow. The party has also said that Islam is incompatible with the German Constitution and vowed mass deportations of immigrants — leading government officials to accuse the party of treating Germans from migrant backgrounds as second-class citizens.

The AfD rejects claims of extremism and says such accusations are politically motivated.

In Saxony-Anhalt, population 2.1 million, many residents see the AfD not as a threat, but a savior, meant to deliver them from unemployment, rising prices and a long list of cultural grievances that stretch back to the reunification of East and West Germany in 1990.

“Our economy is crashing,” Wolfram Adler, 67, a retired train driver, said in an interview this past week in the small town of Haldensleben, “and the AfD is our last chance.”

Experts say the AfD’s support in Saxony-Anhalt is driven by a confluence of forces, many with deep historical roots. The region, in the former East Germany, lost jobs and residents after reunification. Its 8.1 percent unemployment rate is well above the national average. It has the oldest residents, by average age, of any state — and an entrenched sense of mistreatment from the West.

“We are still second-class citizens,” said Ursula Projahn, 74, a retiree from the town of Tangermünde.

AfD supporters in Saxony-Anhalt tend to mistrust democracy and oppose the influx of immigrants that Germany has experienced since 2015, said Marcel Lewandowsky, a political scientist at Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Halle, the state’s second-largest city. Saxony-Anhalt has the second-lowest share, of any state, of residents with a family history of immigration.

Voters in the state also have relatively little affection left for Mr. Merz’s center-right Christian Democrats and his coalition partners, the center-left Social Democrats, out of a sense those parties have done little to improve life in Saxony-Anhalt. Ms. Projahn said the Christian Democrats and another centrist party, the Free Democrats, had disappointed her with poor results, leading her to vote for the AfD this year.

Residents have fewer ties to unions, churches or other social institutions than their counterparts in western states, said Benjamin Höhne, a political scientist at Chemnitz University of Technology, making them more open to messages from parties positioning themselves as outsiders.

Nicolas Spohn, a political scientist at Otto von Guericke University in Magdeburg, said many AfD supporters tell him they back the party because it has never before been in power.

The sentiment, he said, is: “Everything we’ve experienced so far hasn’t worked out the way we imagined it would. We’re disappointed, so let’s let someone who’s never been in this position give it a try.”

The AfD has nurtured that only-we-can-fix-it image with a social media strategy that amplifies long-running local anxieties. Its candidate to govern the state, Ulrich Siegmund, is a state lawmaker and photogenic TikTok star who promises to deport migrants and support native-born German families, so that they can have more children.

He also criticizes the publicly funded news media and Mr. Merz’s center-right and center-left ruling coalition, casting them as corrupt impediments to needed change.

“We’ve now reached a point where we say ‘enough is enough’ — we don’t want to go on like this,” Mr. Siegmund said at a rally this past week. “We want our good, old, safe Germany back at last.”

Opponents have criticized Mr. Siegmund’s plans as unworkable, and as unlikely to deliver the results voters want.

Lisa Heinen, 38, a resident of Saxony-Anhalt who does not support the AfD, said, “People are looking for simple answers to very complex questions, but that doesn’t get us anywhere as a society or as individuals.”

Sven Schulze, the incumbent governor of Saxony-Anhalt and a Christian Democrat, said in an interview this year that “the AfD is really great at describing problems, but not at solving problems.”

The AfD has profited from anger at government restrictions imposed during the coronavirus pandemic, which the party railed against, and more recently, at the wind turbines that dot some of the state’s landscapes.

Some Saxony-Anhalt residents retain sympathies for Russia, including people who feel nostalgia for Communist rule in East Germany, which was backed by the Soviet Union. The sympathy endures amid accusations that Moscow is mounting a campaign of sabotage against German targets in response to Berlin’s wartime support for Ukraine.

The AfD also has warm ties with Russia, to the point that government leaders from other parties have discussed ways to avoid sharing sensitive intelligence with an AfD government should it gain power in Saxony-Anhalt, out of fear it might be passed on to Moscow.

Mr. Adler, like many in his state, said he was angry that federal leaders had moved to stop the flow of cheap Russian natural gas to Germany after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. Electricity prices rose sharply as a result, hampering energy-intensive manufacturers and straining consumers.

“Russia is not my enemy,” Mr. Adler said.

In interviews this past week, many AfD supporters explained their vote in terms that mimic the party’s social media messaging. Frank Krawczyk, 63, a school janitor from Haldensleben, said he believed that ethnic Germans were being replaced by Muslims. He said immigrants can afford to have as many as eight children without having to work, thanks to generous state subsidies, while native-born Germans can afford to have only two, while working. Neither claim is true.

Many also expressed deep dissatisfaction with Mr. Merz, whose popularity has fallen since he took office in May 2025.

Despite those headwinds, Mr. Schulze, the incumbent, could still retain the governorship depending on how many votes the AfD receives and how many parties clear a threshold to claim seats in Parliament.

If the AfD fails to win a majority of seats in the state Parliament, other parties could band together to form a government, most likely led by the Christian Democrats. That would retain the so-called firewall in German politics, where no other major party will work with the AfD. Mr. Siegmund seemed to be preparing his supporters for such an outcome in rallies this week.

But even if the AfD falls short in Saxony-Anhalt, experts said, the forces propelling its rise are unlikely to go away.

“People here in eastern Germany are neither more right-wing than people in other federal states, nor are they more authoritarian than in other federal states,” said Mr. Spohn, the political scientist in Magdeburg. “They’re simply more frustrated.”

item.title: Kenyans Did College Students’ Homework For Years. Then A.I. Arrived.
item.description:
Teresios Bundi once symbolized the strange, life-changing opportunities the internet provided.

Hailing from a farming village in Kenya, Mr. Bundi moved to the capital, Nairobi, in 2011 to be the first in his family to attend university. There, a friend suggested he try a new online job: writing essays for cheating overseas college students.

His first assignment was a two-page essay on the health benefits of the Garcinia cambogia. It was a fruit he had never heard of, and an essay written for a student he didn’t know anything about. He earned $7 for three hours of work.

“That was a lifeline for me, I needed the money,” Mr. Bundi, now 34, said in an interview in Nairobi. He added: “I could not sleep that night. I was ready to burn the midnight oil.”

Mr. Bundi estimates he wrote more than 2,500 essays over the next 12 years, sometimes three a day. He balanced completing his public health degree with helping faraway students studying engineering, medicine and computer science to finish theirs. Some students gave him their school login information so he could keep up with their assignments.

Mr. Bundi didn’t know it then, but he was in the boom era of internet gig work. Newly wired to the global internet and hungry for jobs, well-educated youths from places like Kenya, the Philippines and India found opportunities in the crevices of the digital economy. They could make money online doing unglamorous tasks that others further up the economic ladder did not want to do.

Then A.I arrived, and the good times ended.

In 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT. At colleges worldwide, students made a simple calculation that has become more pronounced today: Why pay a freelancer in Kenya when ChatGPT could do the job?

Essay work began to thin. Rates fell, and assignments dwindled. Before long, the industry shrank to almost nothing. “I never would have expected A.I. could do this,” Mr. Bundi said.

His fate is shared by others who had found a foothold in the global online gig economy. Kenyans also transcribed meetings through the freelance platforms Upwork and Fiverr. They flagged Facebook posts to help the platform decide what could stay up. One after another, those opportunities have withered.

As technologists, economists and policymakers worldwide debate the future of A.I., Kenya’s experience shows how the technology is already dismantling some lower rungs of the global labor market.

“It’s not just going to be Kenya — it’s going to be everywhere we see a big transformation,” said Mark Graham, an Oxford University professor who has studied the global gig economy. “A.I. has come in and taken big chunks of these labor markets.”

Mr. Bundi said he had regrets. When he graduated from college in 2015, he bypassed a public health career to start an online essay-writing business, charging $40 to $70 per paper. Assignments came in through digital platforms, and he divvied up work between himself and students he hired. He rented a house near a university and filled it with desks, fast internet and mattresses. Students worked between classes and slept when too exhausted to write.

Mr. Bundi said he had made at least five times as much as he could earn in public health. He sent money to his parents, coffee farmers who had taken out a loan to buy him a laptop for college.

He sometimes considered the ethics of helping students cheat, but decided it was ultimately their choice. He said he saw himself as a tutor and was proud that a young Kenyan was thriving unnoticed inside Western academia.

Around Nairobi, new money among essay writers was visible. At its peak early this decade, at least 40,000 people in the city were being paid to do other people’s homework, researchers estimated. Essay writers drove new Subarus, carried the latest smartphones and booked exclusive tables at clubs.

After the crash, Mr. Bundi closed his essay-writing business and struggled to find a career path. He is now working for a German government development organization helping young Kenyans find opportunities in the digital economy. He said his experience was a cautionary tale.

“A.I. is coming for bankers, for accountants, it’s coming for engineers, and A.I. will come for architects,” he said. “It’s coming for everybody.”

Few have much sympathy for those aiding an international cheating scheme. But the “essay mills” were, in their way, a Kenyan success story.

More than 100,000 students graduate from Kenyan universities each year into an economy where salaried jobs are scarce. Roughly 80 percent of work is informal — delivery driving, construction, street vending — and youth unemployment is estimated to be over 25 percent. Lack of economic opportunity has fueled a Gen Z-led protest movement.

For a generation with degrees and nowhere to use them, gig work looked like the way out. Kenya’s government thought so, too.

After cheap high-speed internet began arriving around 2009, the government saw online outsourcing — transcription, data entry, graphic design, website development and basic software coding — as a way to climb the economic ladder. Essay writing, while never officially condoned, fit the model.

In 2016, the Kenyan government started a program training university graduates to navigate online freelancer platforms like Upwork. In 2022, the year ChatGPT appeared, Kenya adopted a 10-year National Digital Masterplan that further emphasized outsourcing and online gig work.

“We just wanted jobs,” said Frida Mwangi, 46, who in 2015 turned to transcription work as a path back to the work force while raising four children.

Gig work meant that she could show her daughter that a woman can be a mother and earn a living, Ms. Mwangi said. One big assignment was transcribing interviews of Ellis Island immigrants; she also did medical transcriptions.

That work began drying up in 2017 when transcription software became one of the earliest applications of A.I. Ms. Mwangi’s wages fell, and employers told her to use A.I. and supplement it with her own expertise. She found that process more time-consuming than transcribing on her own, because the A.I. butchered the medical terms. Still, the jobs disappeared.

“My job went completely,” said Ms. Mwangi, who now advocates for better pay and working conditions for gig workers.

Kenya’s outsourcing push brought jobs, but also a backlash. Firms hired by American tech giants faced criticism for low pay and poor working conditions.

That led to a pullback. Sama, a company that hired Kenyans to police user-generated content for Meta, cut back in the country. Scale AI, a start-up that hires people to train A.I. models, discontinued some Kenyan operations.

A.I.’s abilities continue to advance. One test from Scale AI and the Center for A.I. Safety tries to quantify A.I.’s ability to do online freelance work like product design and data analysis. Last October, leading A.I. models completed 2.5 percent of the tasks. By July, they completed 16 percent.

Many who grew up doing essay writing and other gig work are now struggling to find a way back into the labor force.

Alex Munyua, 30, an industrial chemist who worked in the essay business because it was more lucrative, briefly performed data labeling and social media moderation after the industry declined. Now that work has also gone.

“Some have gone back to the villages,” he said. “There are those that tried other sectors, but they were frustrated because they couldn’t get formal jobs.”

Kenya is being buffeted by economic turbulence, with 40 percent of its more than 54 million people living in poverty. Tech jobs are scarce, despite a start-up scene.

Richard Eshilache, 38, built a profitable career in essay writing and said he employed more than 100 writers in 2022. He worked for some overseas students so long that one sent him his diploma.

“He told me it is for the two of us,” Mr. Eshilache said.

He is now trying to embrace A.I. for jobs editing photos and data annotation. None of it pays as well as essay writing.

John Tanui, principal secretary in the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, stood by Kenya’s economic potential as an outsourcing hub, saying it would “unlock opportunities for our young people.”

Yet what jobs remain in essay writing are mainly for “humanizers,” who edit papers written by A.I. to avoid detection from the cheating software used by many universities.

Alphline, who began essay writing in 2021 and gave only her first name for fear of harming future job prospects, said business was as good as ever. With A.I., she can do more work, using the technology to quickly write a first draft and then writing through it herself. She eschews A.I. tools designed to disguise A.I. writing as human, preferring her own touch.

“I can clearly tell a paper that’s A.I. generated compared to one that’s human generated,” she said. “But for a student that doesn’t have that human writing experience, they can get caught.”

For Mr. Bundi, the transition has been difficult. He said he missed the intellectual wrestling match of learning new subjects and writing under a tight deadline, as well as working with some students from when they were freshmen through graduate school.

“It was like getting a parallel education,” he said.

Mr. Bundi sometimes wonders what his life would have been like if he had stayed in public health.

“All my peers that started in 2015 after graduation, they rose through the ranks,” he said. “Now if I go back, I’ll start at an entry level working for somebody who graduated just last year.”

I first heard about Kenya’s essay-writing industry during Covid, when many stuck-at-home students outsourced their homework to people living across the world. Academics lamented the unethical behavior, but it also struck me as fascinating for what it said about globalization and the internet.

It was hard not to have some admiration for the smart young people making some money by doing the hard work that students in the United States, Britain and other English-speaking countries didn’t want to do. As artificial intelligence use exploded, making cheating even easier, my colleague Paul and I wondered about its impact on those writers and other online gig workers. On a recent reporting trip to Kenya, we sat down with several of them.

Edwin Okoth contributed reporting from Nairobi.

item.title: Iran’s State Media Says U.S. Missiles Hit Iranian Oil Tanker Near Kharg
item.description:
Iran’s state media said Saturday that U.S. forces had struck an Iranian oil tanker off the coast of the strategically important Kharg Island, days after the two sides engaged in the most intense fighting in weeks.

The United States has not confirmed the Iranian reports. A spokesman for the U.S. military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Kharg Island, in the Persian Gulf, is Iran’s primary hub for oil exports, which have been squeezed for weeks by a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian news outlets, including the state broadcaster, said that at least one American missile had hit the tanker, and published images of a ship emitting black plumes of smoke.

Tasnim, a semiofficial news outlet affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, reported that the attack took place on Saturday morning, and that the tanker’s crew had survived and were being evacuated.

The reports come as the fate of the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway on Iran’s southern coast, has become central to the conflict between Iran and the United States. The strait previously served as a major shipping route for oil and other key commodities, but Iran has sought to control it since the country was attacked by the United States and Israel earlier this year.

The U.S. Navy has been helping ships navigate a southern route through the strait, near the coast of Oman, drawing retaliation from Iran. On Monday, two oil tankers were attacked within minutes of each other while trying to pass through.

There had been about a month of relative calm in the conflict between Iran and the United States until late August, when the two sides traded fire. This week, U.S. forces carried out a barrage of strikes in retaliation for Iranian attacks on ships and American forces in the region.

One of the strikes hit a wedding in southern Iran, killing five people and wounding dozens, according to Iranian officials.

President Trump issued a renewed threat to Iran on Friday, saying that the United States may strike Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected Iranian nuclear site, “very soon.”

item.title: U.S. Military Sinks Boats Said to Aid Drug Smuggling Near Ecuador
item.description:
U.S. forces operating near Ecuador on Saturday intercepted and destroyed several commercial vessels believed to be used for refueling boats smuggling drugs to the United States.

It was the fourth interdiction of vessels used as floating refueling platforms in the eastern Pacific, according to a U.S. official, who said no one on either side was hurt or killed.

The mission was carried out as part of U.S. Southern Command’s efforts to hinder narcotics smugglers in the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, a campaign that began just over a year ago.

A video posted to social media by the command, which directs military operations in Central and South America, shows a U.S. military vessel, an 11-meter rigid-hull inflatable boat, approach what appears to be a larger civilian craft with fuel jugs lining a raised open deck. A Marine Corps helicopter hovered off the vessel’s starboard side.

The video shows the inflatable boat moving out of the frame, then shows the larger vessel’s bow erupting in an explosion.

People aboard the refueling vessel were transferred to the custody of Ecuadorean government officials, who were nearby as part of the operation, said the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly about the mission.

The operation was supported by sailors and Marines aboard the amphibious ship U.S.S. San Antonio, which launched helicopters that fired munitions into other accompanying vessels and sank them, the official said.

Southern Command, which is based in South Florida, said the refueling operation was run by Los Choneros, which the State Department designated as a “foreign terrorist organization” just days after the campaign against suspected smuggling vessels began on Sept. 2, 2025.

In that time, the U.S. military has launched 68 attacks on what it said were drug smuggling vessels in the region, killing 227 people, according to a New York Times analysis.

item.title: After Months at War, Brief Solace in a Party Town Far From Home
item.description:
After 286 days at sea, the sailors and Marines of the warship Abraham Lincoln savored the pleasures of Pattaya, Thailand. Their indulgences were not all decadent.

They ate Double Super Cheeseburgers at Burger King. They shopped for LeBron James jerseys at the mall. They sipped from fresh coconuts at the beach, their backs to the water where they had spent the last nine-plus months.

And they danced with scantily clad women at nightclubs, the pounding music seemingly even louder than the aural assault of an aircraft carrier at war.

Pattaya is used to welcoming American servicemen. The beach town grew from an R&R refuge for American military personnel during the Vietnam War. For five days beginning on Wednesday, its pool halls, steakhouses and spas, its go-go bars, burrito shacks and trinket stalls have turned their attention to the 5,000 or so service members from the Lincoln, one of four carriers used in the air campaign against Iran.

100 miles

CAMBODIA

Thailand

The New York Times

After a grueling deployment that fed criticism of the Trump administration’s execution of the war, the service members aboard the Lincoln had been instructed not to speak with members of the news media during their time in Pattaya.

Nevertheless, seven sailors confirmed, on the condition of anonymity, that the carrier’s long months at sea, especially without any of the normal stops at so-called liberty ports, had sapped both supplies and morale. They spoke of clogged toilets and, alarmingly, of multiple suicide attempts. (Navy officials have denied an increase in suicide attempts on the Lincoln.) Amid Iranian missile barrages and drone attacks, the half-day shifts merged into a Sisyphean blur, without the usual relief of care packages from home or treats from the ship store.

Meals were rationed, they said, and offered up a monotony of carbs. What she was really craving, one sailor said, was a salad, something green and fresh. Was there one to be had in Pattaya? There was.

The worst, a sailor from Illinois said, was not knowing how much longer they would be at sea. He stopped counting the days at around 200, despairing that the deployment might never end. Another sailor, a New York native, said that he had gone through a dozen deployments without incident, but this time he had watched junior sailors break, one by one. The price of war, he said, was something he was willing to bear, but not when a logistical crisis, which left the carrier with dwindling supplies, seemed preventable.

Did they, he continued — not defining the “they” — think for a moment about the mental health of those aboard the Lincoln? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said that reports of difficult conditions aboard the Lincoln were “misrepresented.” President Trump opined that the Lincoln’s deployment was “not nearly long enough.”

The residents of Pattaya, at least, appeared to understand the hardship borne by the crew of the Lincoln, which will head next toward its home port, San Diego. Pattaya’s mayor turned up to greet the men and women touching dry land for the first time since November. A gem shop offered discounts to the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps personnel. The Sapphire Club, an adult entertainment venue, dispatched three women in strapless black bodysuits to hold placards offering discounts for those with valid U.S. military ID.

At the Tahitian Queen, which bills itself as the oldest bar in Pattaya, circa 1978, Mickey Foth, one of the owners and an American military veteran and former Pentagon employee, teared up as he considered the sacrifices made by the Lincoln’s personnel.

“It’s not just the physical stress, it’s the emotional toll of such a long deployment,” he said, as a line of women in bikinis, one in an American flag pattern, gyrated onstage. “I want to be here, front and center, to say to these men and women, ‘Thank you for your service.’”

On Thursday night, some of the young sailors blushed amid the sexual maelstrom of Pattaya’s Walking Street, with its touts offering intricate shows involving improbably placed pingpong balls. Others, in the throbbing confines of nightclubs, downed shots and leaned close to female companions. Most of the women were Thai, some were Eastern European and Russian, a few were from neighboring countries like Myanmar and Laos or from as far away as Uganda and Uzbekistan.

Prostitution is illegal in Thailand, but you wouldn’t know it in Pattaya. Ever since American bombing missions took off from a nearby Thai air base during the Vietnam War, the village of Pattaya rapidly expanded its red-light district. Business boomed. With the arrival of the Lincoln, local entrepreneurs talked up the positive effect on Pattaya’s economy.

In earlier decades, some women and girls from Thailand’s poor northeast were sold by their families into sex work in Pattaya. While local aid groups say such human trafficking has waned, the criminalization of prostitution, even as it is openly tolerated, can put prostitutes at the mercy of corrupt forces or periodic crackdowns. In the days leading up to the Lincoln’s docking at a nearby port, the police in Pattaya launched an anti-prostitution raid that, like many before it, seemed to have had little lingering effect, apart from stigmatizing the women.

Today, servicemen are a much smaller demographic in Pattaya, compared to tourists from India, China and the Middle East. Amid the sex shows and vendors selling tubes of personal lubricant, vacationing families toted sleeping children, taking in the scene.

“Pattaya has been able to develop itself as a tourist destination, not only for sex tourism but also for culture, temples, family,” said Chanan Yodhong, a gender and sexual equality activist.

On Thursday night, as some sailors and Marines strolled or sat on the curb reeling from too much to drink, a corps of tourist police stood at attention before scattering into the crowds. There were also volunteer officers, residents who are originally from other parts of Asia, Europe and the Middle East.

Among them was Hooman Peseshk, a native of Iran, who has lived in Pattaya for 10 years. He recognized the irony of his patrolling the streets with a shipful of American sailors returning from the war in Iran. But he loved Pattaya, he said, for its status as a free port, where almost anything goes.

“Nobody wants to fight in a war that was started because of our leaders,” he said. “We are all brothers here in Pattaya.”

Despite the beach town’s reputation, many others from the Lincoln said they had no interest in exploring Play Girlz, KINK or the Harem Ultra go-go club. Instead, they dined poolside at the Hilton. They tried out foot spas where little fish nibbled off calluses. At the Hard Rock Hotel, where the minibar comes stocked with chocolate- and strawberry- flavored condoms, a member of the Lincoln crew said he was planning to spend the night ordering room service for one and watching sports on the big-screen TV.

One sailor said that after so many months aboard the carrier — with its frantic sirens, clattering pipes, screaming jet engines, explosive catapult launches — what he missed most was silence. Pattaya is many things, but it is not quiet. For that the sailor would have to wait.

John Ismay contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Huckabee Condemns ‘Terrorist’ Attacks on Palestinians in West Bank Town Hall
item.description:
The U.S. ambassador to Israel denounced on Saturday a rising tide of Israeli extremist attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank, describing the assailants as “terrorists” at a rare meeting with Palestinian Americans in the territory.

The comments by the ambassador, Mike Huckabee, came amid escalating Jewish settler attacks on Palestinians. Last month, settlers besieged the home of an American citizen near Qusra in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, drawing international condemnation.

Mr. Huckabee held a town hall with the mostly Palestinian American residents of Turmus Aya who described life under Israeli military rule, as well as a climate of fear and intimidation created by Israeli settler attacks.

The ambassador said he was “deeply grieved” by their stories, according to a transcript provided by the embassy. He added that he would exert “pressure in order to get some resolution to things you’ve brought up today,” without elaborating.

It was an unusual meeting for Mr. Huckabee, an evangelical pastor and former Arkansas governor whose personal politics have long aligned with Israel’s right-wing settler movement. Several Turmus Aya residents said they could not recall a similar visit by a U.S. ambassador to Israel in recent years, though other U.S. officials have visited before.

The ambassador’s remarks left at least some Palestinian Americans at the meeting disappointed, saying that while he had listened and offered strong words, he was unable to promise concrete change.

“There’s a lot of pain, because I don’t know to whom we can turn at this point,” said Yasser Alqam, a U.S. citizen and local official who helped coordinate Mr. Huckabee’s arrival. “We pinned a lot of hopes on the ambassador’s visit. But he didn’t give us satisfactory answers.”

A spokesman for the Israeli prime minister’s office did not respond to a request for comment on Mr. Huckabee’s remarks.

Attacks by extremist Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the West Bank have surged over the past three years, alongside the Israeli campaign against the militant group Hamas in Gaza.

More than 1,000 Palestinians have been injured during settler attacks since the beginning of 2026, according to the United Nations. Groups of Israeli settlers — often protected by Israeli soldiers — have torched and vandalized buildings, as well as assaulted Palestinian residents.

As the occupying power, the Israeli military is responsible for upholding law and order in the territory. But Israeli rights groups argue that few are prosecuted for the assaults, and say that extremists have largely acted with impunity. Yesh Din, a rights monitor, said just 3 percent of investigations tracked by the group between 2005 and 2025 led to full or partial convictions.

Palestinians and Israeli rights groups also say Israeli troops frequently look the other way when settler attacks happen or at times participate in the assaults.

Mr. Huckabee said he had urged the Israeli government to seek “equal disbursement of justice for every kind of crime.” He suggested that the U.S. Embassy in Israel had limited sway to curb the violence, although he could “influence and call attention to what needs to be corrected.”

“My view is that crime is crime and terror is terror, and it ought to be a consequence to the full extent of the law,” Mr. Huckabee said. Pressed by reporters on whether Israel was doing enough to bring the perpetrators to justice, Mr. Huckabee declined to make an assessment.

After another violent attack in the town of Qusra last weekend, where settlers sieged the house in August, Mr. Netanyahu issued a rare condemnation of the violence and said he expected law enforcement to apprehend the perpetrators.

On Thursday, the Israeli police said it had arrested more than 15 people in recent days for involvement in different attacks across the West Bank, including in Qusra.

President Trump has voiced opposition to Israel annexing the occupied West Bank, although he pushed a peace plan that was widely seen as tilted toward Israel during his first term. Analysts say that the Trump administration now mostly hopes to maintain calm in the territory amid the unresolved six-month-old conflict with Iran and a nominal cease-fire in Gaza frequently marred by violence.

About three million Palestinians live in the occupied West Bank alongside some 500,000 Israeli settlers. Thousands of Palestinian-Americans reside in relatively well-heeled Palestinian towns like Turmus Aya — some year-round, others staying for the summer with their families.

Many had long hoped their U.S. passports would offer some protection from Israeli measures in the occupied territory. But in recent years, they too have felt Israel’s tightening grip on the West Bank and encountered ever more brazen attacks by Israeli extremists.

In the summer of 2023, dozens of Israeli settlers attacked Turmus Aya and other nearby Palestinian communities, setting fires that damaged dozens of cars, buildings and farmland.

Last year, Israeli soldiers gunned down Amer Rabee, a Palestinian American teenager from Turmus Aya, shooting him multiple times in his upper body. The Israeli military accused the teenager and two of his friends of hurling rocks toward the highway and endangering civilians. His family and one of the surviving boys refuted that account.

Mr. Alqam, the local official, said he was disappointed to hear the ambassador suggest that the attackers were a small minority, and he rejected that the United States had limited power over Israel. He noted that, soon after returning to office in 2025, President Trump had removed sanctions that were imposed on extremist Israeli settlers by the Biden administration.

“The United States does have the power to pressure Israel to at least arrest these settlers, who are known to the authorities,” Mr. Alqam said. “They can identify them, one by one.”

The town hall was hosted at the home of Sameer Barakat, a Palestinian American who moved back to the West Bank from Dallas earlier this year. Mr. Barakat said his home had already been attacked with rocks, leading him to place barbed wire on the exterior.

“What I want to say to Mr. Huckabee is that we need protection for Americans here,” Mr. Barakat said ahead of the town hall. “They are protected everywhere except in Palestine.” Your responsibility is to protect us.”

item.title: Chinese Worker Rescued From Tunnel in Nepal 10 Days After Floods
item.description:
A Chinese worker was rescued on Saturday from a tunnel in Nepal, the Nepali Army said, 10 days after its entrance was buried in the catastrophic floods that tore through one of the country’s northern river systems.

The army said that a joint rescue team, including foreign personnel, had pulled the man from inside a 740-foot tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project. “His health is currently being assessed, and further search and rescue operations are continuing,” the army said in a statement. It did not immediately confirm the man’s name.

At least 1,200 people were killed in the disaster last week, when a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent tsunami-like waves through valleys along the border of Nepal and the Tibet region of China. Another 5,000 people are missing.

Rescue efforts in recent days have become focused on the hundreds of men who were working underground at the time of the disaster, building the power stations that form the basis of Nepal’s budding hydropower industry.

Unlike the thousands of people who were living alongside the rivers, the workers trapped underground, it was hoped, might have been able to shelter from the force of the flood and find enough air and fresh water to survive beyond the 72-hour window after which rescuers estimate that the chances of survival usually drop off.

On Friday, that hope was at least partially vindicated when two Nepali workers were found alive in a tunnel below the Upper Trishuli 3A project, downriver from the site of Saturday’s rescue. One of the men, Sanjay Sah, estimated that there had been 40 or 50 others at his work site when the disaster struck. He knew of no others who might still be living, he said.

In February, the deputy director of the labor ministry in Nepal told local media outlets that about 1,600 Chinese citizens were living in Nepal on work permits. That made China the biggest source of foreign workers in Nepal — not counting India, which sends its citizens back and forth across the Nepali border freely.

Chinese engineers are especially visible at Nepal’s hydropower and other infrastructure projects.

South Korea has an especially large investment in the Upper Trishuli-1 project, one of the most productive hydropower plants in the area. A 44-member Korea Disaster Relief Team has been working in the afflicted districts of Nepal since Tuesday.

item.title: Trump Envoys Arrive in Moscow for Talks on Ukraine War
item.description:
President Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday, Russian state news agencies reported, ahead of a planned trip to Kyiv, Ukraine, as they hope to reignite diplomatic efforts to end the war there.

Mr. Witkoff, the president’s special envoy, and Mr. Kushner, Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, are making their first trip to Russia since January. A month after that visit, U.S.-backed peace negotiations went into a deep freeze when the United States and Israel attacked Iran.

Since Mr. Trump took office in January 2025, Mr. Witkoff has met regularly with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. At the end of that year, Mr. Kushner began joining Mr. Witkoff for meetings with the Russian leader.

But the planned trip to Kyiv would be the first by either American envoy.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said on Friday that Ukrainian forces would not conduct airstrikes on Russia while the envoys were there, and he called on Mr. Putin to reciprocate by temporarily halting strikes on Ukraine.

The U.S. envoys’ visit to the Russian capital is taking place days after the C.I.A. director, John Ratcliffe, traveled there. Mr. Ratcliffe delivered a bleak assessment of Moscow’s prospects in the war and urged Russian officials to end it.

The talks follow a shift in the war’s dynamics. Since April, Ukraine has launched a campaign targeting Russian fuel and logistics infrastructure, bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians.

Russia, for its part, has taken advantage of Ukraine’s depleted arsenal of air defense interceptors, allowing it to strike more targets across the country and making daily life in Kyiv increasingly dangerous. On Friday, a drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s domestic intelligence service in the heart of the Ukrainian capital.

Russia and Ukraine also face mounting financial strain to support a war that is growing costlier, as both sides struggle to keep pace with advanced technologies, like jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles.

But the war appears far away from any resolution.

Speaking on Friday, Dmitri S. Peskov, Mr. Putin’s spokesman, praised “the good will of the Americans” who, he said, “are ready to continue their mediation efforts.” But Mr. Peskov said Russia would continue to insist that Ukraine withdraw its troops from the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, in the country’s east, before any cease-fire could occur — a demand that Ukraine has rejected.

Mr. Peskov’s comments followed statements on Thursday by Mr. Putin, who said that regardless of American mediation efforts, “Russia and Ukraine must first reach an agreement between themselves.”
